Think about it, when you are configuring a game for your build, there are many game settings. They work on levels like Low, Medium and High. These terms are very confusing, especially with PC having wide configurations and games coming from all sorts of time periods.

A game from 2008's Ultra is not the same as 2016's ultra, so why are they called the same thing.

We need harder levels of optimization in game settings. Game settings that work on hard numbers based on benchmarks, and the devs work specifically with each level of graphics.

This is what game settings should look like:

CPU core count: 1,2,4,6,8

CPU bench level: 1000, 3000, 6000

RAM level: 4GB,6GB,8GB,12GB,16GB

Vram level: 1GB,2GB,4GB,8GB,12GB

Antialiasing method: FXAA,SMAA,MSAA,SSAA

GPU bench level: 5000,10000,15000,20000

FPS Target:30,60,120,144,240,500

These settings will allow game developers and artists to ensure that everyone gets a consistent experience (of course without downgrading people with better hardware) throughout their gameplay, and give people certainty their configuration works with their settings without screwing around until they find the sweet spot. These settings should also be configured pre-download to ensure that textures are only scaled down once and have the best quality possible for anything lower than ultra.

This is the only advantage consoles have over PC, and it is so easy to stop, so why can't we have consistent, standardized settings which all games use, which will make things easier for everyone?

I'm graduating soon from University in my small Texas town, and want to move to a larger city somewhere north. I want to go somewhere that has more activities and events going on for the weekends, and someplace with a decent nightlife that I can hopefully find and meet interesting people though.

I've been to Chicago before, but that was in the summer when the weather was nice. I'm not sure how things would be in the Winter. I really enjoyed the time I spent literally a block away from Grant park, but I'm not nearly as familiar with the rest of the city.

I spent a day in Seattle last New Year and had a pretty good time, but didn't get to spend time there extensively like in Chicago. Seattle, at least for the brief time that I was there, seemed to have a little less hospitality/well mannered people than I saw in Chicago. There seems to be a deeper divide in the city between the upper/lower class parts of town, although I'm sure that also exists in Chicago and I probably just didn't see it as much.
